newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon government expected to win confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon government expected to win confidence vote.

text.p: Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's government came under renewed attack in parliament on Wednesday but was expected to win a vote of confidence later in the day.

Parliamentary sources expected about 100 of the 128 deputies to support Hariri's Syrian-backed government installed earlier this month. Up to 20 opposition MPs said they will vote against it at the end of the debate.

Hariri, a 52-year-old billionaire tycoon leading Lebanon's revival from the 1975-90 civil war, and members of his 29-man cabinet listened patiently as deputies took turns in criticising the government's policy statement.
"Hariri's methods are behind Lebanon's impoverishment," opposition MP Mustapha Saad said, declaring that he would not vote for the government.
Christian deputy Pierre Dakkash said he would also vote against the government -- Hariri's third since 1992 -- accusing many of its members including Hariri of being the cause of Lebanon's ills.
"The current government, with its leader and its solid nuclus of key ministers, are responsible for the condition that the country has come to and for what citizens complain of," Dakkash said.

Citing a U.N. report that one million Lebanese, a third of the population, live under the poverty line, he asked: "Where are the economic, social, housing, health and educational plans and programmes?"
Replying to the criticism, Hariri said the U.N. report was based on 1970s data.

"True there are social problems and solving them is very important...but I assure you these figures are incorrect and the country is being depictd as if people are begging on the street. That is not so.
"Poverty in Lebanon is among the lowest in the Arab countries apart from the oil states," Hariri said.
The government's policy statement sets social policies as a priority, emphasising housing, medicare, social security and transportation as well as agriculture, industry and tourism.

Christian MP Nabil al-Boustani said that keeping a tight rein over monetary stability in Lebanon -- the main theme of Hariri's previous two governments -- did not mean that the country's economic situation was healthy.
"There is a crisis of economic and living conditions... because productive investments are very small," Boustani said.

A number of deputies have rapped the government over a media law that slashes the number of private television and radio stations in the country -- licencing a few stations mostly owned or controlled by Hariri or other government figures.

Opposition groups and trade unions have called a general strike and demonstration on Thursday to protest against the media law, a ban on demonstrations imposed by Hariri three years ago, and his perceived lack of social policies.
